newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Child sex scandal report puts Belgium on the spot.
newsitem.headline: Child sex scandal report puts Belgium on the spot.

text.p: A parliamentary report into the bungled investigations of Belgium's child abduction, abuse and murder scandal has put the government on the spot, warning it that the legal basis of the state was under threat.

"The malfunctioning of the Belgian penal system today poses serious problems that put at grave risk the state of law," the commission said, proposing the creation of a single, federal police force to replace the existing three, rival forces.
The report follows six months of hearings after convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux led police in August to the buried bodies of four young girls. He has been charged with murder.
A fifth girl was found dead last month. Convicted child molester Patrick Derochette has been charged with rape leading to death.

The commission, whose often televised investigations gripped and disgusted the nation, revealed incompetence and bitter rivalry between the gendarmerie, judicial police and communal police that meant key information was often jealously guarded.
It also accused investigating magistrates of sloth, and a complete failure to co-ordinate the investigations or liaise properly with the parents of the missing children.
Pushed by a protest march in October of more than 250,000 people through the streets of Brussels, the government has promised a series of reforms.

It has promised a review of the early release of sex offenders -- Dutroux and Derochette were both paroled -- as well as proposing that a magistrate is automatically and immediately appointed to the case when a child goes missing.

It has also pledged to abolish the political promotion of magistrates, more clearly define the tasks of the different police forces, promote the rights of victims and to set up a special centre for missing children.
But the parliamentary commission went even further.

"In the realm of criminal justice we are witnessing a phenomenon that is at once historic and unique: Our citizens have mobilised today for justice. It is from this movement that justice will come," the report said.
Apart from the complete reorganisation of the police forces, the commission proposed a series of other reforms.
- Victims must be taken seriously from the outset. In many of the cases the missing children were treated as runaways for several days.
- Victims and their families should automatically be given legal assistance. In some cases the parents were strongly advised not to appoint a lawyer.
- Close contact should be created and maintained with the families. In many instances the families were kept completely in the dark about the investigations.
- Victims of sexual abuse should be consulted about the parole from prison of their attackers.
- Investigators should be better trained and better directed.

- There should be a legal framework governing the running of informants. Some of the people who have been charged in the scandals so far were police informers, and there have been suggestions their controllers might have deflected investigators in order to protect them.
- Public prosecutors and magistrates should be under close supervision, trained better and made to shoulder all their responsibilities.
- There should be clear and open lines of communication between the judiciary and the police.
- The whole judicial establishment should be streamlined and brought up to date.

The commission's report will be debated in parliament on Thursday and Friday this week. The public will be watching closely to see how it is received and if there are any signs that party politics will try to subvert its thrust.
The commission itself will carry on working until September 30 on its hypothesis that the criminals exposed so far may have had high level protection -- a view held by many people.
